docs.title: curfew
docs.text:
curfew is a Kubernetes operator that puts workloads to sleep on a cron schedule, then brings them back. Use it to switch off non-production workloads at night and on weekends.

  • Deployments, StatefulSets and any other kind with a /scale subresource are scaled to 0.
  • CronJobs are suspended.
  • The replica count before sleep is remembered and restored on wake-up.

docs.title: In one example
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
  annotations:
    curfew/sleep: "0 20 * * 1-5"     # scale to 0 at 20:00, Monday to Friday
    curfew/wake: "0 8 * * 1-5"       # restore at 08:00, Monday to Friday
    curfew/timezone: "Europe/Paris"  # optional, default UTC

This Deployment sleeps every weekday night and all weekend, from Friday 20:00 until Monday 08:00.

docs.title: What else it does
docs.text: Namespace schedules One schedule for every workload in a namespace, with exclusions by kind or label Holidays Skip sleep and wake on listed dates, so a long weekend stays asleep Keep awake Keep a workload or a namespace up until a given time, without touching its schedule Waves Stop workloads in order, such as an app before its database, and wake them in reverse Other kinds Schedule Argo Rollouts or any custom resource with a /scale subresource Dry run See what curfew would do on a cluster before letting it act Metrics Prometheus metrics, including the CPU and memory freed while workloads sleep

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: Install curfew with its Helm chart, then add a schedule to a workload.

docs.title: Where replica counts are kept
docs.text:
Original replicas are stored in the ConfigMap curfew-state in the operator's namespace, with one key per workload: <kind>.<namespace>.<name>. To see what is asleep:

kubectl get configmap curfew-state -n curfew -o yaml

Order of writes: on sleep, the count is saved before scaling to 0. On wake, the workload is scaled up before its entry is removed. A failure in between is retried and never loses the original count.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text: What happens What curfew does Annotations removed from a sleeping workload Wakes it right away Sleeping workload deleted Removes its entry Sleeping workload scaled up by hand Saves the new count and scales it back to 0. Remove the annotations, or set curfew/awake-until, to keep it up. 3 times in one sleep window points to another controller. Workload already at 0 at sleep time Stores nothing; it stays at 0 on wake CronJob asleep Suspended (spec.suspend: true): it starts no new Jobs, but Jobs already running are not stopped. A CronJob counts as 1 replica while it runs and 0 while suspended, so one you suspended yourself stays suspended after wake. Namespace starting with kube- Ignored, along with its workloads, even when annotated Invalid annotation (cron, time zone, date) Logged as an error; the workload is left as it is. Fixing the annotation triggers a new check. Invalid stored count (negative, not a number, too large) Logged and dropped; the workload is not scaled Operator uninstalled Sleeping workloads stay at 0. curfew-state survives helm uninstall, and a reinstall wakes them on schedule.

docs.title: Running more than one replica
docs.text: Leader election is always on: with replicaCount above 1, only the leader acts, and another replica takes over if it goes away.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Requirements: Go 1.27, just, Docker and Helm. Python 3 for this documentation site.

just test            # go test -v ./...
just test-race       # with the race detector
just lint            # golangci-lint v2
just vuln            # govulncheck: known vulnerabilities in dependencies
just check           # fmt, vet, lint, test, vuln
just install-tools   # install golangci-lint v2
just docker-build    # build the image (VERSION=x.y.z to set the version)
just docker-buildx   # multi-arch image (linux/amd64, linux/arm64)
just helm-deploy     # create the labeled namespace, install or upgrade the chart
just deploy          # uninstall, rebuild the image, reinstall

The namespace defaults to curfew. Set OPERATOR_NS to change it.

docs.title: Local cluster with Colima
docs.text:
Colima runs a local Kubernetes (k3s). Images built with Colima's Docker are available to it without a registry.

just colima-up         # colima start --kubernetes
just e2e               # build, deploy, then run test/e2e.sh (about 5 minutes)
just colima-logs       # follow the operator logs
just colima-undeploy   # uninstall (the curfew-state ConfigMap is kept)

test/e2e.sh runs in a throwaway curfew-e2e namespace and checks that:

  • a Deployment, a StatefulSet and a CronJob sleep and wake on real cron times a few minutes ahead, and their counts are stored then cleared,
  • the StatefulSet, in wave 1, waits for the Deployment's pods to be gone,
  • curfew/awake-until wakes a sleeping workload, and removing the annotations wakes it right away,
  • a namespace schedule applies, with StatefulSets excluded,
  • a Widget custom resource (test/widget-crd.yaml, enabled through test/e2e-values.yaml) sleeps and wakes through /scale.

KUBE_CONTEXT (default colima) selects another cluster. CI runs the same test on kind.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
This site is built with Material for MkDocs from docs/ and mkdocs.yml, and published to GitHub Pages on every push to main.

just docs-serve   # http://127.0.0.1:8000, reloads on edits
just docs-build   # build into site/, failing on broken links

docs.title: Code layout
docs.text:
• cmd/root.go: CLI entry point, logging and tracing setup
  • internal/curfew/:
    • curfew.go: controller setup and the reconcile loop
    • schedule.go: which rule applies and when (schedules, exclusions, holidays, keep awake)
    • wave.go: waves
    • metrics.go, conflict.go: metrics and detection of other controllers
  • internal/values/: annotation names and constants
  • internal/telemetry/: OpenTelemetry tracer setup
  • helm/: the chart
  • mocks/: sample annotated manifests for manual testing
  • test/: end-to-end test and its fixtures

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
curfew runs inside the cluster only. Install it with the Helm chart in the repository's helm/ folder, in its own namespace, labeled with the restricted Pod Security level:

git clone https://github.com/paloth/curfew.git && cd curfew
kubectl create namespace curfew
kubectl label namespace curfew pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
helm upgrade --install curfew helm/ --namespace curfew

From a checkout, just helm-deploy runs the last three steps.

Keep the namespace to admins

Anyone who can write in curfew's namespace can change the replica counts sleeping workloads get back, or stop the operator. See Security.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
Set them with --set or a values file (helm/values.yaml lists them all):

Value Default What it does image.repository / image.tag ghcr.io/paloth/curfew / chart appVersion Operator image. Use an immutable version tag. replicaCount 1 Operator pods. Leader election is always on, so more than one is safe: only the leader acts. dev false Debug logs dryRun false Decide and log without changing any workload (see Dry run) extraKinds [] More kinds to schedule, such as Argo Rollouts (see Other kinds) watchNamespaces [] Namespaces curfew may act in. Empty means the whole cluster. networkPolicy.enabled true Restricts the operator pod's network traffic networkPolicy.apiServerPorts [443, 6443] Ports the API server listens on metrics.enabled false Prometheus metrics on port 8080, with a Service (see Metrics) metrics.serviceMonitor false Also create a ServiceMonitor (needs the Prometheus Operator) tracing.endpoint "" OTLP HTTP host:port for traces. Empty disables tracing (see Tracing). tracing.insecure false Send traces over plain HTTP instead of TLS resources 10m CPU, 64Mi request, 256Mi limit The operator caches every workload it watches. Raise memory on big clusters.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
helm uninstall curfew --namespace curfew

Sleeping workloads stay at 0. The curfew-state ConfigMap, which holds their replica counts, is created by the operator rather than by Helm, so it survives the uninstall. A reinstall picks it up and wakes the workloads on schedule.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text:
Set dryRun=true to try curfew on a cluster before letting it act:

helm upgrade --install curfew helm/ -n curfew --set dryRun=true
  • Every scale and suspend is sent to the API server with dryRun=All: it is checked, permissions included, but not applied. Log lines carry "dryRun":true.
  • curfew-state is still written, so the logs show the wake-ups too.
  • Waves don't wait, since nothing really stops. curfew logs Would wait for wave and goes on.

Turning dry run off mid-sleep is safe: the stored count matches the running replicas, and curfew scales them down.

To follow what curfew would do:

kubectl -n curfew logs deploy/curfew -f | grep -E 'Scaling down|Waking up'

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Set metrics.enabled=true to serve Prometheus metrics on port 8080, behind the curfew-metrics Service. Add metrics.serviceMonitor=true if you run the Prometheus Operator.

helm upgrade --install curfew helm/ -n curfew --set metrics.enabled=true --set metrics.serviceMonitor=true
Metric Labels What it counts curfew_sleeping_workloads namespace, kind Workloads asleep, from curfew-state curfew_scale_total kind, direction (sleep/wake), result (ok/error) Scale and suspend requests, dry-run ones included curfew_scaled_up_while_asleep_total namespace, kind Sleeping workloads found scaled up again and scaled back to 0 (see Other controllers) curfew_freed_cpu_cores namespace, kind, name CPU requests a sleeping workload gives back: stored replicas × its pod's requests curfew_freed_memory_bytes namespace, kind, name Same, for memory

What curfew saves right now, cluster-wide:

sum(curfew_freed_cpu_cores)
sum(curfew_freed_memory_bytes) / 2^30   # GiB

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Only the leader reports curfew_* metrics. Other replicas expose controller-runtime's own metrics only.
  • After a restart, the numbers come back as the first reconciles run, within seconds.
  • Freed resources count regular containers only, not init containers. CronJobs and other kinds are not counted.

No authentication

The endpoint is plain HTTP without authentication, and the NetworkPolicy opens port 8080 to every namespace. The metrics show namespace and workload names.

To look at them by hand:

kubectl -n curfew port-forward svc/curfew-metrics 8080
curl -s localhost:8080/metrics | grep curfew_

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The chart creates:

  • A ClusterRole:

    • get, list, watch on Deployments and StatefulSets
    • get, update, patch on their /scale subresource only
    • get, list, watch, patch on CronJobs
    • list on Pods, to know when an earlier wave is fully stopped
    • for each of the extraKinds: get, list, watch on it, and get, update, patch on its /scale

    For Deployments and StatefulSets, curfew can change nothing but the replica count. CronJobs have no subresource for suspend, so curfew needs patch on the CronJob itself; it only ever patches spec.suspend.

  • The binding for that role:

    • watchNamespaces empty: a ClusterRoleBinding, so curfew acts in the whole cluster.
    • watchNamespaces set: one RoleBinding per listed namespace, so curfew acts only there. It also watches only those namespaces. Each one must exist before you install.
  • A ClusterRole to read namespaces, for namespace schedules, in both modes.
  • A Role in the operator's namespace:
    • create ConfigMaps, and get/update on curfew-state only
    • Leases, for leader election
    • Events

docs.title: Why curfew needs its own namespace
docs.text:
• Anyone who can edit the curfew-state ConfigMap decides which replica count a sleeping workload gets back.
  • Anyone who can edit the curfew-leader Lease can stop the operator.
  • In a shared namespace such as default, that hands these powers to everyone with write access there.

docs.title: Pod hardening
docs.text:
• Non-root numeric user (65532), read-only root filesystem, no privilege escalation, all Linux capabilities dropped, and the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile. This passes the restricted Pod Security level.
  • The NetworkPolicy allows incoming traffic only on the health port (9090), plus the metrics port (8080) when metrics are on. Outgoing traffic is allowed only to the API server ports, DNS (port 53) and the trace collector's port. It only takes effect if your network plugin enforces NetworkPolicy, as k3s and Calico do.

docs.title: Supply chain
docs.text:
• Base images in the Dockerfile are pinned by digest, and GitHub Actions by commit SHA.
  • just vuln runs govulncheck on the dependencies; CI runs it on every pull request.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
Set tracing.endpoint to an OTLP HTTP collector, such as Jaeger on port 4318:

helm upgrade --install curfew helm/ -n curfew \
  --set tracing.endpoint=jaeger-collector.observability:4318

Each reconcile (one check-and-fix pass on a workload) creates a Reconcile span with the kind, namespace and name. It has child spans LoadState, SaveState and Scale.

Export uses TLS by default. For a collector without TLS, such as a plain in-cluster Jaeger, add --set tracing.insecure=true.

The chart's NetworkPolicy opens the endpoint's port for outgoing traffic.

docs.title: Local Jaeger
docs.text:
From a checkout, just jaeger-up starts Jaeger with Docker Compose. The UI is at http://localhost:16686.

Your cluster must be able to reach your machine, which is often host.docker.internal:4318 with kind or Docker Desktop. Set tracing.insecure=true for it.

docs.title: Holidays
docs.text:
Cron can't say "not on public holidays". List those days instead, next to the schedule:

metadata:
  annotations:
    curfew/sleep: "0 20 * * 1-5"
    curfew/wake: "0 8 * * 1-5"
    curfew/skip-dates: "2026-12-24,2026-12-25,2027-01-01"

No sleep or wake happens on a listed day, so the workload keeps the state it was in when the day started. With this schedule, a workload stays asleep:

  • from Wednesday 23 December at 20:00 until Monday 28 December at 08:00,
  • and from Thursday 31 December at 20:00 until Monday 4 January at 08:00.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Dates are read in the schedule's curfew/timezone.
  • curfew/skip-dates belongs to the schedule. On a namespace, it applies to the workloads that follow the namespace's schedule. A workload with its own curfew/sleep needs its own curfew/skip-dates.
  • Exact dates only: no ranges and no yearly repeats, so update the list each year.
  • An invalid date is logged and the workload is left as it is.

To keep workloads awake on a day they would sleep, use Keep awake instead.

docs.title: Keep awake
docs.text:
Working late? Keep a workload, or a whole namespace, awake without touching its schedule:

kubectl annotate deployment my-app curfew/awake-until=2026-10-28T08:00:00+01:00
kubectl annotate namespace staging curfew/awake-until=2026-10-28T08:00:00+01:00
  • Until that time the workload counts as awake: a sleeping one wakes right away, and nothing goes to sleep. After it, the schedule applies again.
  • A namespace's curfew/awake-until covers all its scheduled workloads, those with their own schedule included. A workload's own curfew/awake-until wins over the namespace's.
  • The time is RFC 3339 and needs a zone: Z or an offset such as +01:00.
  • An invalid value is logged and the workload is left as it is, as with other invalid annotations.
  • An expired annotation does nothing. curfew does not remove it, so you can leave it or delete it:
kubectl annotate deployment my-app curfew/awake-until-

docs.title: Namespace schedules
docs.text:
Put the schedule annotations on a namespace to apply them to every workload in it:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: staging
  annotations:
    curfew/sleep: "0 20 * * 1-5"
    curfew/wake: "0 8 * * 1-5"
    curfew/timezone: "Europe/Paris"
    curfew/exclude-kinds: "StatefulSet"           # optional
    curfew/exclude-labels: "tier=data,keep-alive" # optional

docs.title: Which rule a workload follows
docs.text:
A workload in that namespace follows the first rule that applies:

  1. Its own rule: a workload with its own curfew/sleep uses its own curfew/sleep, curfew/wake, curfew/timezone and curfew/skip-dates, and ignores the namespace's.
  2. Excluded: the namespace's rule is skipped for a workload whose kind is listed in curfew/exclude-kinds, or whose labels match an entry of curfew/exclude-labels.
  3. The namespace's rule.
Annotation Format curfew/exclude-kinds Comma-separated kinds, any case: Deployment, StatefulSet, CronJob, or one of your other kinds curfew/exclude-labels Comma-separated entries: key=value (that exact value) or key (any value). One matching entry is enough.

docs.title: Changes apply at once
docs.text:
Changing or removing the namespace annotations re-checks every workload in it. Workloads that are no longer covered, because the schedule was removed or they became excluded, are woken up.

Namespaces starting with kube- are ignored, along with the workloads in them.

curfew/awake-until on a namespace works even without a namespace schedule: it keeps every scheduled workload in it awake, those with their own schedule included.

docs.title: Other controllers
docs.text:
curfew changes the replica count. Anything else that sets it puts the workload back up, curfew scales it down again, and the two loop all night.

curfew notices: after 3 scale-ups in one sleep window it logs another controller is likely fighting curfew, and the curfew_scaled_up_while_asleep_total metric counts every one. The count is kept in memory, so a restart of the operator starts it over. A scale that keeps failing and being retried counts too.

docs.title: Argo CD
docs.text:
With self-heal on, Argo CD resets replicas to the value in Git. Tell it to leave the field alone:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
spec:
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      jsonPointers: [/spec/replicas]
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions: [RespectIgnoreDifferences=true]

Or leave replicas out of the manifest.

docs.title: KEDA
docs.text: KEDA owns the replica count of the workloads it scales. Don't schedule those with curfew: pause them through KEDA instead, with the autoscaling.keda.sh/paused-replicas: "0" annotation on the ScaledObject.

docs.title: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
docs.text: Nothing to do: an HPA does nothing while its target is at 0 replicas, and takes over again once curfew restores it.

docs.title: Other kinds
docs.text:
Any kind with a /scale subresource can be scheduled too, such as Argo Rollouts. List it in the chart's values:

extraKinds:
  - group: argoproj.io
    version: v1alpha1
    kind: Rollout
    resource: rollouts   # the plural name, used for permissions

curfew then reads the same annotations on them, and namespace schedules, curfew/exclude-kinds (Rollout) and waves cover them too.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• The chart grants get, list, watch on the kind, and get, update, patch on its /scale only.
  • In waves, curfew waits for the pods matching the selector that /scale reports. Readiness on wake is status.readyReplicas when the kind has it, else the replica count /scale reports.
  • They are not counted in the curfew_freed_* metrics.

Install the CRD first

The kind's CustomResourceDefinition must exist before curfew starts. If it doesn't, curfew fails to start.

KEDA ScaledObjects are not supported this way: see Other controllers.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
Add the annotations to a Deployment, StatefulSet or CronJob (or one of your other kinds):

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
  annotations:
    curfew/sleep: "0 20 * * 1-5"     # scale to 0 at 20:00, Monday to Friday
    curfew/wake: "0 8 * * 1-5"       # restore at 08:00, Monday to Friday
    curfew/timezone: "Europe/Paris"  # optional, default UTC
Annotation Required Format curfew/sleep yes Standard 5-field cron (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week) or a descriptor like @daily curfew/wake yes Same as sleep curfew/timezone no IANA time zone name, e.g. America/New_York. Default UTC. curfew/skip-dates no Comma-separated dates (YYYY-MM-DD). No sleep or wake on those days (see Holidays). curfew/awake-until no RFC 3339 time, e.g. 2026-10-28T08:00:00+01:00. Stay awake until then (see Keep awake). curfew/wave no Integer, default 0. Order of sleep and wake within a namespace (see Waves).

Both schedules are read in the given time zone.

The example above sleeps from Friday 20:00 until Monday 08:00: after Friday's sleep, the next wake time is Monday, so the workload stays down all weekend.

docs.title: How curfew decides
docs.text:
At any moment curfew looks at which comes next, the next sleep or the next wake:

  • Wake comes first: the workload should be asleep now.
  • Sleep comes first: the workload should be awake now.

It then schedules its next check for exactly that time. Adding the annotations during a sleep window scales the workload down right away.

docs.title: Waking up
docs.text:
• At wake time, curfew restores the replica count it stored at sleep time.
  • Removing the annotations wakes a sleeping workload right away.
  • A workload that was already at 0 at sleep time stays at 0.

Behavior covers the details, such as scaling a sleeping workload by hand or deleting it.

docs.title: Waves
docs.text:
Some workloads must stop in order, such as an app that needs to shut down cleanly before its database stops. Give them a wave, like Argo CD sync waves:

metadata:
  annotations:
    curfew/wave: "1"   # any integer, negative included; default 0

Wave 1 on the database is enough: the app (wave 0) stops first, and the database comes back first.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Waves only order workloads of the same namespace.

  • Sleep goes up the waves: -1, then 0 (workloads without the annotation), then 1, and so on. A workload waits until every lower-wave workload that is also going to sleep is fully stopped:
    • Deployments, StatefulSets and other kinds: at 0 replicas with no pods left, terminating ones included.
    • CronJobs: suspended, with no running Jobs.
  • Wake goes down the waves. A workload waits until every higher-wave workload that is also waking up is back and ready.

Workloads moving the other way, or not scheduled, don't hold anyone back.

docs.title: Waiting
docs.text:
• A waiting workload is checked again every 10 seconds, and logs Waiting for wave with the workload it waits for.
  • After 10 minutes it stops waiting, logs Wave timeout, proceeding, and goes ahead, so one stuck pod can't keep the rest up all night.
  • If the operator restarts or changes leader, the 10 minutes start over.
  • In dry run, nothing really stops, so waves don't wait: curfew logs Would wait for wave and goes on.
